pages.headline: Grow the book without betting it on the lateral market.
pages.outcome: Your growth plan currently has one engine: add lawyers fast enough to keep up with the matters the firm wins, and hope the pyramid holds. Governed AI adds a second engine. Retrieval, drafting, and assembly move onto rails inside privilege boundaries, partner attention returns to winning matters and standing behind positions, and the book can grow faster than headcount without the firm's name paying for it.
triggers: The growth plan assumes lateral partners and senior associates the market will not supply at a price the model affords.
Partners are at capacity while demand keeps arriving, and the choice reads as decline matters or dilute supervision.
The firm's best work product lives in a few heads and in matter files nobody can search, and succession is a hope rather than a plan.
Clients have started asking what the firm's AI posture is, and the current answer depends on which partner they ask.

evidence.text: ABA Formal Opinion 512 (July 2024) sets out the duties a lawyer using generative AI must fully consider: competence, confidentiality, communication, supervision, meritorious claims, candor toward the tribunal, and reasonable fees. It sets the competence bar where a firm can operationalize it: a reasonable understanding of the specific tool's capabilities and limits, not becoming an AI expert.
evidence.caveat: The opinion interprets the ABA Model Rules; state adoption and state opinions vary, and nothing here is legal advice. It defines the duties, not the operating model. Building the operating model is the growth decision on your desk.

evidence.text: In a preregistered experiment published in Science, access to a general AI assistant cut time on occupation-specific professional writing tasks by about 40 percent while raising judged quality by about 18 percent (N of about 453).
evidence.caveat: Task-level results on general professional writing, not legal drafting under privilege and not full matters. Quality was evaluator-scored on experimental outputs. Do not treat as firm-level realization or margin improvement; treat it as the reason first-draft turnaround is worth baselining.

evidence.text: The field experiment that reported AI gains on tasks inside its capability frontier also reported professional quality falling when AI was relied on for tasks outside that frontier.
evidence.caveat: Consulting tasks at one elite firm, not legal work, and where the frontier sits shifts with the model and the domain. In a law practice the outside-frontier failure looks like a fabricated citation or a conclusion never checked against authority, which is why verification stays a written step with a name on it.

Governed AI operations gives you the architecture: matter-scoped access, approved sources, provenance by default, and a sanctioned path fast enough that nobody wants the shadow one.

pages.headline: An AI posture the firm can defend: to clients, to courts, and to itself.
pages.outcome: The risk is not that lawyers use AI. It is that the firm cannot say how, where, under what controls, and inside which boundaries. Governed AI operations replaces improvisation with a defensible posture: client and matter walls that mirror ethical screens, a named attorney answering for every output, verification of every cited authority as procedure rather than assumption, and an answer checked against each client's guidelines before anyone asks.

evidence.text: ABA Formal Opinion 512 (July 2024) confirms that a lawyer's existing duties, competence, confidentiality, communication, supervision, meritorious claims, candor toward the tribunal, and reasonable fees, apply in full when generative AI is used. pages.headline: An AI investment case built for a firm that bills by the hour.
pages.outcome: You have seen the vendor math: hours saved multiplied by a blended rate, payback by the second month. In an hourly firm that arithmetic is not just optimistic, it is confused, because a saved hour is not revenue until someone decides where it lands. The governed version is different by construction: baselines before pilots, program cost counted once, adoption lag priced in, ranges instead of points, and freed capacity named to a destination, more matters, alternative-fee margin, client development, before it is counted as anything.
triggers: AI spend is accumulating across practice groups with no consolidated view of cost, let alone return.
A vendor business case multiplied saved hours by a blended rate and did not survive ten minutes of partner questions.
Realization and write-downs are drifting in ways utilization alone no longer explains.
The next planning cycle needs an AI line item, and there is no defensible number to put on it.

evidence.text: In McKinsey's 2025 State of AI survey (N=1,993), 64 percent of respondents said AI is enabling innovation while only 39 percent reported EBIT impact at the enterprise level.
evidence.source: McKinsey / QuantumBlack, The State of AI, 2025
evidence.caveat: Cross-industry, global, self-reported rather than audited, with large-organization bias and the publisher's own commercial interest in AI services; not a law-firm benchmark. In an hourly firm the gap is wider still, because a saved hour is not margin until the partnership decides where it lands. Only a baseline and honest measurement can show what happened in your firm.
